sources.title: Human History Map: Malaysia index and imported border features
sources.note: Local index and every imported Malaysia feature were checked directly. The index begins in 1920; features cover 1920-1938 and 1945-2020, with an actual 1938-1945 gap. The same simplified present-day-style outline excludes Singapore throughout and leaves Kuching outside its Sarawak edge. Brunei is separately mapped.

sources.title: Government of Malaysia: Malaysian History
sources.note: Official history page checked for Japanese occupation, the 1946 Malayan Union, the 1948 Emergency, the 1956 London Agreement, Malayan independence on 31 August 1957, and formation of Malaysia on 16 September 1963. Its celebratory tone is treated as the government's presentation, not independent evaluation.

sources.title: Parliament of Malaysia: General Information and parliamentary history
sources.note: Official parliamentary chronology checked for the 1957 Constitution and independence, constitutional monarchy, the bicameral Parliament opened in 1959, the Malaysia Agreement, and declaration of Malaysia on 16 September 1963. Institutional description is not evidence that access to political power has always been equal.

sources.title: United Nations Treaty Collection: Agreement relating to the separation of Singapore from Malaysia
sources.note: Official treaty record checked: agreement signed at Kuala Lumpur on 7 August 1965 and entered into force on 9 August 1965, when Singapore became an independent and sovereign state.

sources.title: Malaysia Ministry of Economy: Third Malaysia Plan chapter on New Economic Policy goals and strategy
sources.note: Original government planning chapter checked for the 1969 racial conflict, the Rukun Negara response, and New Economic Policy goals after the conflict. Policy intentions are identified as official aims, not accepted as proof of equal outcomes.

sources.title: World Bank: Malaysia overview, updated April 2025
sources.note: Original World Bank overview checked for the transformation from commodities to manufacturing and services, electrical and electronics exports, income and health gains, inequality and learning challenges, and the 2017 green sukuk. Figures retain the source's dates.

sources.title: Malaysian Investment Development Authority: Malaysia's electrical and electronics industry
sources.note: Official investment-agency industry history checked: eight component manufacturers established operations in the 1970s, followed by an industry spanning semiconductors and consumer and industrial electronics. The account is promotional, so no unsupported ranking or local-invention claim is adopted.

sources.title: Malaysia Ministry of Economy: Thirteenth Malaysia Plan, 2026-2030
sources.note: Original official plan checked for its 2026-2030 scope and stated priorities in semiconductor reform, education, health, regional balance, innovation and environmental sustainability. Targets are described as plans, never completed results.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Archaeological Heritage of Niah National Park's Caves Complex
sources.note: Full UNESCO entry checked for at least 50,000 years of rainforest interaction, archaeological deposits, rock paintings, boat-shaped burials, and living molong harvesting practice. Ancient evidence is clearly separated from achievements of the modern federation.

sources.title: UNESCO: Breakfast culture in Malaysia
sources.note: Full indexed UNESCO entry checked for nasi lemak, roti canai and teh tarik, home and public meals, multi-ethnic participation, affordability and intergenerational transmission. It documents a broad living practice without claiming every person eats the same breakfast.

sources.title: UNESCO: Songket
sources.note: Full indexed UNESCO entry checked: supplementary gold or silver thread, two-pedal kek loom, months of work, women's weaving, men's equipment-making, intergenerational learning, and ceremonial uses including weddings and births.

sources.title: UNESCO: Pantun
sources.note: Full indexed UNESCO entry checked: common four-line a-b-a-b form, themes of love, family, community and nature, use at weddings and ceremonies, formal and informal teaching, and polite indirect expression. Inscription date 2025 is not presented as the tradition's origin.

sources.title: Malaysia Ministry of Home Affairs: Federal Constitution in Malay, Article 152
sources.note: Official Malay government printing checked for Article 152 and the exact Roman-script sample 'Bahasa kebangsaan ialah bahasa Melayu'. The statement that this displayed sample reads left to right is direct inspection of the cited printing, not a claim that Malay has only one writing tradition.

sources.title: Judicial Appointments Commission Malaysia: Federal Constitution in English, Article 152
sources.note: Official English government PDF checked at printed page 122/PDF 123, Article 152(1): 'The national language shall be the Malay language', followed by protection for using, teaching and learning other languages outside official purposes.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia: Education for every child in Sabah, 25 July 2024
sources.note: Full original story checked for stateless children, community-created Alternative Learning Centres, the island school built on stilts, reading and texting, music, and mothers teaching sewing. Individual examples are not generalized to every Sabah family.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia: Learning
sources.note: Full programme page checked for education barriers involving documentation, disability, distance, cost and language, especially for Orang Asli and other Indigenous children, and for work supporting mother-tongue and alternative learning.

sources.title: Malaysia Ministry of Health: History of family health services
sources.note: Official ministry chronology checked for maternal and child health as the core of rural services, the 1956 three-tier referral system, later integration into primary care, electronic records, and mobile bus and boat clinics. Aspirational universal-coverage language is not treated as measured universal access.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia: Going mobile to reach children in rural Sabah, 5 May 2023
sources.note: Full original account checked: Sabah Health Department-led convoy to three Kemabong villages, medical and dental care, five-hour walking access to the closest clinic, 4x4 terrain, and teenagers climbing a hill for connectivity. This is one outreach mission, not nationwide access.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia and Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia: Impact of Climate Change on Children, 2021 synthesis report
sources.note: Original 99-page report checked at printed pages 30-31/PDF 41-42 and printed page 53/PDF 64-65: dated national water and sanitation estimates, exclusions from official statistics, disaster disruption, wastewater treatment and marginalized-community gaps.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia: A safe space for children on Kota Kinabalu's streets, 30 September 2022
sources.note: Full original account checked for the Sabah government and partner-supported centre serving citizen and non-citizen children aged 7-15 with basic lessons, snacks, showers, ramps and accessible toilets. The centre's services are not generalized to all undocumented children.

sources.title: UNICEF Malaysia: Surrounded by Water, Yet None to Drink, 22 August 2025
sources.note: Full dated family account checked for recurrent flooding in Rantau Panjang, evacuation to a school shelter without water or electricity, sanitation risks, and a child's habit of lifting books to safety. This family story illustrates a risk rather than a national average.

Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Malaysia from colonial territories to a modern federation, with independence, industrial and scientific work, shared breakfasts, family crafts, schools, healthcare and the everyday importance of safe toilets.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Modern Malaysia card with explicit pre-state context. The imported index begins in 1920, but the Federation of Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957 and Malaysia formed with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore on 16 September 1963; Singapore separated on 9 August 1965. Seven imported features cover 1920-1938 and 1945-2020, leaving a real 1938-1945 display gap. All tested outlines use essentially the same present-day-style shape: Kuala Lumpur, Sibu, Miri and Kota Kinabalu are included; Singapore and Bandar Seri Begawan are excluded; Kuching is incorrectly outside the simplified Sarawak edge. Brunei and earlier Malay, Malacca and Malaysian Islamic-state records remain separate. No invented predecessor, fall or successor link.
